variants.name: nlohmann::json conversion functions (modern default)
variants.implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: declare to_json/from_json for the entity in its namespace and the library converts it to and from a JSON document in one call (json j = entity; entity = j.get<Entity>()); the payload then goes into a TEXT/JSONB column through the data layer. The NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_* macros generate the pair for simple structs, but hand-written functions are the honest form once fields move or defaults matter. The classic alternative is Boost.Serialization, which serializes the object graph - including pointers and versioned classes - into an archive; choose it when the payload is a graph rather than a flat record or when class-version compatibility is required.
pitfalls: from_json must use at() (or the WITH_DEFAULTS macros) instead of operator[]: operator[] on a missing key inserts a null and the later extraction throws or misleads.
Raw C-style char arrays do not round-trip through the default conversions (written as a string, expected as an array); use std::string or std::array<char, N>.
Renaming or reordering keys silently breaks existing readers; keep a version key (or a versioned schema) and validate on load.

variants.name: Boost.Serialization archive with class versioning
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Serialization writes the object graph into an archive tied to a stream: a serialize() member (or free function) lists fields with the & operator, base classes are written through base_object, and BOOST_CLASS_VERSION plus the version argument let a reader branch on what it finds in older payloads. Choose it over JSON when the payload is a real graph (polymorphic pointers, shared nodes are de-duplicated) or when explicit class versions are required, and pick the text archive for rows that outlive a single build.
pitfalls: Calling a base class serialize() directly instead of base_object<> skips instance tracking and version information, silently producing archives that cannot be read back correctly.
The archive holds a reference to its stream: destroying the stream before the archive (or vice versa) truncates or corrupts the payload.
Binary archives are not portable across endianness or compiler/runtime versions - prefer the text archive for long-lived rows.
